title: Police search the whole band at Los Angeles station
summary: Plainclothes officers search everyone, finding nothing, and watch the band for the six weeks in Los Angeles.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: And a good thing they did, because after these two incidents... A couple of days later, when we arrived in Los Angeles at this train station, we walked... Everybody's getting their bags off the train, after a ride like that you're tired and you want to get to a hotel and a bath... We started walking to this place where you get taxicabs. And out there... Well, I didn't notice anything at first. And then this guy tapped me on the shoulder! He said, "Can I speak to you a minute?" I said, "Man, no. I'm tired. I've been riding two days." And it was a White guy, you know.. I didn't know what he wanted and didn't care. I said, "I've
been riding two days; I want to get..." And he tapped me again, and then he showed me his badge.

I said, "Oh!" I turned around and went back into a room with him in the station. When I got back there, everybody was back there. All the members of the band, every last one of them was in this room. Because apparently, they just made a major swoop. The only two people who didn't get stopped were Sarah and Gene Ammons. And they must have been pretty fast, because they got away.

Anyway, I went back in this room, and the guy said, "Now, what you do is open your bag and lay it out." They had people in there, these guys went through these bags with a fine-tooth comb. Then there was another room where you went in there and you had to take your clothes off, and they went through your clothes. Luckily, everybody had done exactly what Billy Eckstine had told them to do, and nothing was found.

But we were in Los Angeles for a good six weeks, and the whole time we were out there, there were plainclothesmen hanging around the hotels, there were plainclothesmen hanging around the club where we worked, and they just kept their eyes on us the whole time.
Well, before these two incidents happened, the band had kind of had a reputation. Everybody knew that all these wild kids was doing everything they could think of. Socially we

weren't very well accepted, you know! I remember many times we played theatres, when they had guys back there painting or doing maintenance work, where the manager had told Billy, "Tell the boys to be quiet, because some of these men are watchin' you'all."
